Interviewer: Welcome to Community Voices. Today we are talking about a new public art programme in Muscat. With me is Aisha, who coordinates the programme, and Kareem, a student volunteer. Aisha, what is the main idea behind the project?
Aisha: We want young people to feel that art belongs to everyone. A painting in a gallery can be wonderful, but we also believe that art can make everyday public places more welcoming. So we invited students to create temporary displays for the waterfront walk and several community centres.
Interviewer: Why temporary displays rather than permanent ones?
Aisha: We wanted to test different ideas before making long-term decisions. Temporary installations are also easier to adapt. For example, the first outdoor display used fabric panels, but the wind damaged some of them. We replaced them with strong recycled boards, and the result was much better.
Interviewer: Kareem, what did your team create?
Kareem: We designed a series of photographs showing traditional skills alongside modern jobs. We interviewed a boat builder, a digital designer and a young engineer. Each person explained how patience and creativity matter in their work. The photographs are accompanied by short captions in Arabic and English.
Interviewer: Did you have previous experience of photography?
Kareem: Not much. I had taken photos on my phone, but I had never organised an exhibition. A local photographer taught us how lighting changes the mood of an image. We have been improving our pictures for three months, and I can see a real difference.
Interviewer: How did visitors respond?
Aisha: We collected feedback from nearly two hundred visitors during the first weekend. Most appreciated the chance to learn about local occupations. Some suggested that we add audio descriptions for people who cannot see the photographs easily. We have already started preparing those descriptions.
Interviewer: Was the project expensive?
Aisha: We had a small grant, but our main resources were people's time and donated materials. Several shops provided boards and printing at a reduced price. The volunteers did not receive payment; they received training and certificates instead.
Interviewer: What happens next?
Kareem: We are planning workshops at three schools next month. Students will make their own mini-exhibitions. We hope the project encourages them to ask questions about their communities rather than simply copy images they see online.
Interviewer: Finally, what is your advice for a student who wants to help?
Aisha: Begin with a question that matters to your community. Listen to different opinions, test an idea on a small scale and be willing to change it. Great projects rarely succeed perfectly on the first attempt.

Good morning. My name is Dr Salma Rashid, and today I will describe how a university team is helping our town prepare for a changing climate. I will focus on four areas: water, buildings, transport and education. Our purpose is not to predict every detail of the future. Instead, we want to make choices that will protect people under a range of possible conditions.
First, let us consider water. Five years ago, the university began collecting temperature and rainfall information from different parts of the region. The researchers noticed that rainfall was becoming less predictable, even though some individual storms were unusually heavy. Rather than planning only for average rainfall, the team suggested systems that could store water safely after sudden storms. Last year, a pilot project installed collection tanks beside two public buildings. The water is used for trees and gardens, not for drinking.
Second, we looked at buildings. During the hottest months, cooling can consume a large amount of electricity. Architecture students compared the performance of several designs. Buildings with shaded windows and improved insulation required less energy to maintain comfortable indoor temperatures. The students also learned an important lesson: a solution that works in one building may not work in another. They therefore measured actual performance instead of relying only on computer predictions.
Third, our transport study asked how people travel to school, work and shops. More than six hundred residents completed an online questionnaire. Many said that they would walk more often if streets had reliable shade and safer crossings. Others wanted buses with clearer schedules. The researchers recommended improving existing routes before investing in a completely new transport system. A small trial will begin near the university in September.
Finally, we explored education. Technology is useful, but it cannot replace informed decisions. School students joined a series of practical workshops. They measured the temperature of shaded and unshaded surfaces, compared household water use and designed posters explaining their findings. Their most successful posters used clear numbers and avoided frightening claims that could not be supported by evidence.
What can we learn from these projects? Good planning combines scientific measurements with the experience of local people. It also requires patience. The university will publish its next report in December, but the work will continue after that date. Students who wish to participate can register through the university's community office. Volunteers do not need advanced scientific knowledge; curiosity, careful observation and willingness to work with others are enough. Applications close on the final Friday of August. After registration, volunteers attend a short introduction where staff describe safety rules, explain the project goals and answer questions. Everyone receives a clear schedule, and participants can choose activities that match their available time. Thank you for listening.

Presenter: Welcome to Student Voices. Today we are discussing how young people can prepare for life after school. Our guests are Fatma, a careers adviser, and Yousuf, a Grade 12 student. Fatma, why should students begin thinking about their future before their final exams?
Fatma: Because decisions become easier when students understand their interests and strengths. A career is not simply a job title. It involves the skills people use, the problems they solve and the kind of environment in which they work.
Yousuf: I used to think that choosing a career meant selecting a university subject immediately. Then I attended a workshop where we interviewed people from different professions.
Presenter: What surprised you?
Yousuf: An engineer told us that she spends much of her day communicating with other people. I had imagined engineers working alone with machines. She said teamwork is essential because large projects require many different specialists.
Fatma: That is a useful discovery. Students sometimes focus on marks and forget the importance of practical experience. Volunteering and short workplace visits can help them discover what they enjoy.
Presenter: Is work experience easy to arrange?
Fatma: Not always. Some workplaces cannot accept students because of safety rules. Schools can still invite professionals to speak or arrange supervised activities.
Yousuf: Our school organised a problem-solving challenge. Teams had to design a simple shelter using recycled materials. We had limited time, and our first design collapsed.
Presenter: What did your team do next?
Yousuf: We listened to one another, changed the structure and tested it again. Our final shelter was not the biggest, but it was stable. I learned that mistakes can help us improve.
Presenter: What advice would you give students who are uncertain?
Fatma: Keep your options open, collect reliable information and ask thoughtful questions. University is one possible route, but professional training and other pathways can also lead to rewarding work.
Yousuf: I would add that students should not copy their friends' plans. I am now interested in environmental engineering because it combines scientific knowledge with helping communities.
Presenter: Finally, how can parents support this process?
Fatma: They can listen without making every decision for their children. Discussing different possibilities calmly often leads to better choices.
Presenter: Thank you both. Our next programme will explore how digital tools are changing education.

When I was sixteen, our school announced a regional science competition. I had always enjoyed building small electronic devices, so I decided to enter with a project that measured soil moisture. My original idea was to help gardeners know when plants needed water. I worked on the device every afternoon, using parts borrowed from the science laboratory.

Two weeks before the competition, I tested the device in our school garden. The results were confusing. Sometimes the display showed that the soil was dry even after watering. At first, I blamed the electronic sensor. I replaced it, checked the wires and repeated the experiment, but the problem continued.

My teacher advised me to write down every measurement rather than depend on memory. I created a simple table with the time, soil conditions and readings. When I compared the information, I noticed that the device behaved differently in direct sunlight. The sensor itself was working, but its position made the readings unreliable.

I moved the sensor deeper into the soil and added a protective cover. The next tests were more consistent. Unfortunately, correcting the design took longer than expected, and I still needed to prepare my presentation. A friend offered to help me make a clear diagram showing how the system worked. We practised explaining the project in everyday language without using too many technical terms.

On the day of the competition, I was nervous. Other teams had built impressive robots and complicated models. During the judging, one examiner asked what I would do if the device stopped working. I explained the tests that had failed and the changes I had made. To my surprise, she seemed more interested in my problem-solving process than in the appearance of the finished model.

My project did not win first prize. It received a special award for careful testing and practical value. More importantly, I learned to record evidence, accept advice and explain my work clearly. Later, a local gardening group asked whether I could demonstrate the device at one of their meetings. That invitation showed me that a small school project could be useful outside the classroom.

I still keep the first faulty sensor in a box. It reminds me that progress often begins when something goes wrong and we take the time to understand why.

Interviewer: Welcome to Future Horizons. Today we are talking about a student project that connects creative design with environmental awareness. Our guests are Noor, an art teacher, and Hamad, a student who worked on the exhibition. Noor, how did the project begin?
Noor: It began when our class visited a coastal nature reserve. We saw an area where discarded plastic had collected near the shore. Students wanted to do something useful, but we also wanted them to think about how art can communicate important messages.
Interviewer: What did the students decide to make?
Noor: Instead of producing ordinary posters, they created sculptures from cleaned, recycled materials. Each sculpture represented a different sea animal, and a small card explained why that animal was important to the ecosystem.
Interviewer: Hamad, which part did you work on?
Hamad: My group built a model of a sea turtle using plastic bottle tops and pieces of cardboard. At first, we tried using glue, but the parts did not hold together well. A local craftsperson showed us how to join the pieces with wire.
Interviewer: Did that solve every problem?
Hamad: Not immediately. Some pieces were still too heavy. We changed the design and used lighter materials. We also tested it outdoors because the exhibition would be held in an open courtyard.
Interviewer: Who visited the exhibition?
Noor: Students, parents and several community volunteers. About three hundred people attended over two days. Many visitors said the sculptures helped them understand how waste can affect marine life.
Interviewer: What happened to the sculptures afterwards?
Noor: A few were displayed in the school library, but most materials were separated for recycling. We did not want the project itself to create unnecessary waste.
Interviewer: What was the biggest lesson for you, Hamad?
Hamad: I learned that being creative is not just having an unusual idea. It also means listening to advice, solving practical problems and working with people who have different skills.
Interviewer: Are there plans for another exhibition?
Noor: Yes. Next term we hope to work with two neighbouring schools. This time the students will choose the environmental issues themselves, then research the facts before they begin designing.
Interviewer: Thank you, Noor and Hamad. It sounds like a project where art and science really support each other.

Good morning, everyone. I am Dr Laila Al Balushi, and I have been asked to report the findings of our student study on digital learning. The study took place in four secondary schools and focused on how young people use technology to improve their English. We wanted to understand not only which tools were popular, but also which activities students considered genuinely useful.

We began in February with a questionnaire completed by eight hundred students. Most respondents used educational videos at least once a week, while many also used vocabulary applications. However, students were less confident about checking whether information found online was reliable. This was an important finding, because convenient access to information does not guarantee that it is accurate.

The second stage involved classroom observations. Teachers noticed that students often remembered new expressions better when they practised them in a meaningful conversation. Simply repeating isolated words was less effective. As a result, several classes began using short role-play activities after watching educational videos.

We also spoke to teachers about their concerns. The main issue was not a lack of devices. It was the time needed to choose suitable material and plan lessons that included active participation. A group of experienced teachers therefore prepared a shared collection of recommended resources. The collection is available through the regional education centre.

Students asked for clearer feedback on their writing. In response, the research team tested a system that highlighted possible grammar errors and suggested areas for improvement. The tool did not assign final grades. Teachers continued to assess the quality of ideas, organisation and language use themselves.

Our report recommends three practical steps. First, schools should teach learners how to evaluate online sources. Second, digital activities should include opportunities to communicate rather than only watch or read. Third, teachers should receive time to review new resources before using them in class.

The complete report will be published in November on the education centre's website. Next March, the team hopes to return to the participating schools and examine whether these changes have helped students become more confident and independent learners. Anyone interested in assisting with the follow-up study should contact the research office by email. We welcome teachers and university students who are willing to observe lessons or help analyse anonymous survey responses.

Thank you for listening. I look forward to discussing your questions after the presentation.

Noura: Good morning, Salim. I heard that your class is preparing an exhibition about traditional jobs and new technology. How did the idea begin?
Salim: We visited the old harbour and interviewed people who repair fishing boats. Our teacher asked us to compare their working methods with those of modern designers.
Noura: That sounds interesting. Did the workers agree to speak to students?
Salim: Most were very welcoming. One boat builder explained that he learned his craft from his father, but now uses computer drawings to plan repairs.
Noura: So he combines traditional knowledge with modern tools?
Salim: Exactly. We realised that new technology does not always replace older skills. Sometimes it helps people preserve them.
Noura: What did your group decide to display?
Salim: We created photographs, short videos and models made from recycled cardboard. Each display explains one practical skill and how it has changed.
Noura: Was collecting information easy?
Salim: Not at first. We found conflicting information on several websites, so we checked details with local experts instead of copying everything online.
Noura: How did you divide the work?
Salim: Two students conducted interviews, three prepared the visual materials and the rest edited the explanations. Everyone had to check the final text for accuracy.
Noura: Did you face any problems?
Salim: The video recording was interrupted by strong wind. We arranged another interview inside the workshop and used a small microphone.
Noura: What did you learn from that difficulty?
Salim: We learned to have a backup plan and to listen to feedback. Our second recording was much clearer.
Noura: When can visitors see the exhibition?
Salim: It opens next Thursday in the school hall. We will invite families and neighbouring classes during the afternoon.
Noura: Is there an entrance fee?
Salim: No, admission is free. However, visitors can donate used books for the community reading corner.
Noura: Are there any activities for younger pupils?
Salim: Yes. We have prepared a simple matching game where children connect tools with the jobs that use them.
Noura: What are you most proud of?
Salim: The cooperation between generations. Students and experienced workers learned something from one another.
Noura: Would you organise a similar project again?
Salim: Definitely, but next time I would start the interviews earlier and allow more time for editing.
Noura: Thank you, Salim. I hope the exhibition encourages more students to explore their community.
Salim: Thank you for inviting me. We look forward to welcoming everyone.

Last year, I decided to take part in a weekend hiking challenge with my school outdoor club. I was excited because I had never explored the mountain trail before. Our teacher explained that the purpose was not to reach the finish line first, but to practise planning, cooperation and respect for the environment. We divided into small groups and checked our equipment before leaving.

On the first morning, the weather was cool and the sky was clear. My group carried water, maps and a small first-aid kit. We stopped regularly to identify local plants and photograph unusual rock formations. By midday, we had reached a narrow path overlooking a valley. Our guide reminded us to stay together and avoid leaving marked trails.

After lunch, one of my friends noticed that his water bottle was missing. We searched our bags and realised he had probably left it at the previous rest stop. We were concerned because the afternoon was getting warmer. Rather than sending him back alone, our group leader contacted the guide, who checked the route and arranged for two adults to look for the bottle. Meanwhile, we shared the extra water we had brought.

The bottle was found near a large tree, but the delay meant that we could not complete the original route before sunset. Our teacher discussed two possibilities with us. We could rush towards the final viewpoint or use a shorter, safer path to the campsite. Everyone agreed that safety was more important than finishing the entire distance.

That evening, we cooked a simple meal together and reflected on the day. At first, I felt disappointed about missing the viewpoint. Then I realised how much I had learned. Checking equipment was important, but so was staying calm when plans changed. I also appreciated that our group had made decisions together rather than blaming the person who lost his bottle.

The following morning, the guide showed us a different trail with excellent views of the mountains. We returned to school in the afternoon and prepared a short presentation for younger students. We explained how to pack carefully, follow instructions and protect natural places. I still want to visit the original viewpoint someday, but I now understand that a successful adventure is measured by what we learn and how responsibly we act.

activities.script: Mariam helped organise a community learning project at the public library. The aim was to offer students a meaningful opportunity to investigate a practical problem, discuss solutions and learn from local experience. The organisers began by consulting pupils and neighbours. Their first discussions showed that different people had different needs, so they avoided making decisions before collecting reliable evidence. A small team prepared a timetable and shared responsibilities. Some members interviewed visitors while others checked resources, studied costs and wrote instructions. They met regularly to compare their progress. During the first trial, unexpected difficulties affected the schedule. A change of weather and a shortage of equipment forced the team to adjust its plans instead of abandoning the whole project. Several volunteers suggested practical improvements. They wanted clear signs, more accessible activities and simple explanations that younger pupils could understand without specialist knowledge. The team collected anonymous feedback after the event. Most participants valued the opportunity to learn by doing, although a few said that they needed more time to ask questions. Teachers explained that success should not be measured only by attendance. Students also needed to show that they could apply knowledge, explain their decisions and cooperate responsibly. After reviewing the results, the organisers published a short report. They planned another event the following term and invited neighbouring schools to exchange ideas and resources. Students used a shared notebook to record what they observed, including details that challenged their first assumptions. Instead of copying information from one website, they checked several sources and asked a local expert for advice. At the end of each meeting, the group agreed on a realistic next step. This made it easier for everyone to understand what still needed attention and prevented small misunderstandings from becoming larger problems. The experience reminded participants that useful projects rarely succeed immediately. Careful planning, patient communication and a willingness to change direction were essential throughout the work.
